text:
“Cut it, Commander. Window’s closing,” Houston barked, voice tight with static and stress.

Onboard *Orion-7*, Captain Elara Vance didn’t look at the countdown. She stared at the flickering pressure gauge on Fuel Line B—a micro-anomaly she’d caught two cycles ago that ground sensors had dismissed as noise. “Negative, Control. The valve is sticky. If we launch with a partial seal, we risk structural failure during max-Q.”

“Sensors say it’s green!” The CAPCOM’s frustration spiked, audible over the hum of life support. “We lose the window, we lose the mission timeline for six weeks. Do you want to explain that to Congress? To your family?”

“I want to come back home alive,” Elara snapped, her gloved hand hovering over the abort switch. The seconds ticked: 03:00... 02:58... The ship groaned, straining against its tethers like a caged beast eager to run.

Elara saw the telemetry spike. A whisper of vibration no computer filter wanted to acknowledge. “Hold position. Thirty more seconds.”

“Commander, stand down! You’re holding up millions in funding!”

“Money buys insurance,” Elara said coldly, finally turning her eyes from the gauge to the viewport, watching the sun crest over Florida’s horizon. “It doesn’t buy oxygen.”

00:01.
